Busyness as a Status Symbol

忙碌为何成了身份象征

OriginalFull translation

[A] One of my bad habits is saying “busy” when people ask me how I’m doing. Sometimes it’s because I actually am busy, but other times it’s because that’s what I think I’m supposed to say. That’s what important people say. That’s what people who get promoted say. But working long hours doesn’t drive better results. Never taking a vacation won’t lead to a promotion. So why are we so proud to talk about how busy we are all the time?

[B] In 2016, researchers from Columbia, Harvard, and Georgetown conducted a study to figure it out. They found busy people are perceived to be of high status, and interestingly, these status attributions are heavily influenced by our own beliefs about social mobility. In other words, the more we believe that one has the opportunity for success based on hard work, the more we tend to think that people who skip leisure and work all the time are of higher standing.

[C] That’s why we feel like we have to appear busy, and there’s a real perception that if someone is knee-deep in meetings, emails and stress, then they’re probably a big deal. This culture of busyness is making it hard for employees to find work-life balance. According to a recent study, one in five highly engaged employees are at risk of burnout.

[D] Personally, I’m going to stop saying “busy” when people ask me how I am. It sounds self-righteous and sets the wrong tone. Phrases like “I have limited access to email” and “I’ll respond as soon as I get back” sound like you’re being held against your will from working as opposed to making the most of your time off.

[E] That’s why we recently launched the Out of Office Email Generator, a free tool you can use before your next long weekend or trip. You can share loud and proud that you won’t be checking email until you’re back. Managers need to think twice about emailing their teams on the weekend and talking about how busy they are. Leaders should take time off themselves and encourage employees to do the same.

Full translation

[A] 我的一个坏习惯是，别人问我近况如何时，我总说“忙”。有时是因为我确实很忙，但有时是因为我觉得自己就应该这样回答。重要的人都这么说，得到晋升的人都这么说。然而，长时间工作并不能带来更好的成果，从不休假也不会让你获得晋升。那么，我们为什么总是如此自豪地谈论自己有多忙呢？

[B] 2016 年，来自哥伦比亚大学、哈佛大学和乔治敦大学的研究人员开展了一项研究，试图弄清这个问题。他们发现，人们认为忙碌的人社会地位较高。有趣的是，这种地位判断在很大程度上受我们自身对社会流动性的看法影响。换句话说，我们越相信一个人有机会通过努力工作取得成功，就越倾向于认为那些放弃休闲、一直工作的人地位更高。

[C] 这就是为什么我们觉得自己必须表现得很忙。而且，人们确实普遍认为：如果一个人深陷会议、电子邮件和压力之中，那他大概是个重要人物。这种推崇忙碌的文化，使员工难以在工作与生活之间找到平衡。根据最近的一项研究，每五名工作投入度很高的员工中，就有一名面临职业倦怠的风险。

[D] 就我个人而言，别人再问我近况如何时，我不会再说“忙”了。这样的回答听起来自以为是，也传递了不恰当的态度。“我不方便经常查看邮件”和“我一回来就会回复”之类的话，听起来仿佛你是被迫无法工作，而不是在充分利用自己的休假时光。

[E] 这就是我们最近推出“休假自动回复邮件生成器”的原因。这是一款免费工具，你可以在下一次长周末或旅行前使用。你完全可以大大方方、自豪地告诉别人：回来之前，你不会查看邮件。管理者在周末给团队发邮件，或谈论自己有多忙之前，都应该三思。领导者应当自己带头休假，并鼓励员工也这样做。
